chunks: Al-Hasan ibn Mahbub from Abu Ayyub from Amr ibn Uthman from Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) said:

I said to Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), 'Is intercourse disliked at a specific time among the times?' He said, 'Yes, it is disliked on the night in which the moon is eclipsed, and the day in which the sun is eclipsed, and between the setting of the sun until the redness (shafaq) disappears, and from the rising of the dawn until the rising of the sun, and during the black wind, the red wind, the yellow wind, and the earthquake.'

And indeed, the Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him and his family) spent the night with one of the women, and the moon was eclipsed that night, but he did not have intercourse with her. His wife said to him, 'O Messenger of Allah, by my father and mother, is all this for dislike?'
He said, 'Woe to you, this is the event in the sky, so I disliked that I should enjoy myself, so I would enter into something [of the eclipse].'
And indeed Allah reproached a people, saying, Exalted and Majestic is He: 'And if they see a fragment of the sky falling, they say, 'It is a cloud piled up.'

And by Allah, whoever does not have intercourse during these times that I have described will not be granted offspring from his intercourse, and he has heard this hadith and sees what he likes [as a sign].

key_terms.اَلشَّفَقُ: The redness in the sky after sunset

ai.seo_question: What are the specific times and events during which marital intercourse is considered disliked in Shia jurisprudence?
ai.summary: Imam al-Sadiq (peace be upon him) delineates specific times of *makruh* for marital intercourse, including eclipses, twilight periods, and natural phenomena like winds and earthquakes, grounding this in the Prophet’s practice of abstaining during a lunar eclipse to avoid mixing pleasure with celestial awe. The narration references Quran 7:137 to illustrate human reaction to celestial signs, while concluding that avoiding intercourse during these blessed moments ensures the offspring are granted success and virtue, a concept deeply rooted in Shia juristic discussions on *takhayyur* (choosing the best time for conception).
